# Do Written Procedures Help an AI Assistant? Every company has the colleague who "just knows" how things are done. Then they go on holiday, and nobody can raise a purchase order. Writing it down is the cure. But does writing it down help an **AI**? That is the question for this post. ## The idea In [Part 3](/posts/bcsupplychain3/) the AI wrote notes in its wiki after every run: how Business Central behaves, what went wrong, what it assumed. The idea I want to test is simple. If those notes are turned into proper **procedures**, will the next run need less reasoning and make fewer mistakes? I borrowed a distinction from quality management. There are two kinds of document, and people mix them up all the time. | Document | Answers | Written for | In this project | |---|---|---|---| | **Standard procedure** (an SOP) | What, why, who decides, which facts must be collected | The person who owns the process | "Create a draft purchase order": the facts to collect, the guardrails, the steps that only a person can do | | **Work instruction** | Exactly how to perform one task, click by click | The person doing the hands-on work | "Create a purchase order with one line": the exact tool, the parameters that worked, the errors and their fixes | A step in an SOP links to the work instruction that performs it. I wrote three SOPs and five work instructions from what the AI had already learned, plus what I knew about the API. Here is how the AI uses them: ```mermaid flowchart LR CL["CLAUDE.md
read the procedures first"] --> IDX["Procedures index"] IDX --> SOP["SOP
what, why, who decides,
which facts to ask for"] SOP --> WI["Work instruction
exact tool, fields, known errors"] WI --> DO["Do the task"] DO --> HO["Hand-over note"] DO -. "new gotcha found" .-> WI ``` Look at the dotted line at the bottom. When the AI hits a new problem, it writes the fix back into the work instruction. The procedures grow with use. :::brain-power SOP or work instruction? Which document does each line belong in? Decide first, answers are underneath. 1. "Never raise a credit limit." 2. "Use the child create tool first. The flat one was rejected." 3. "Ask all missing facts in ONE round." 4. "`documentNumber` is not a property of a sales line. Use `documentId`." **Answers:** 1 and 3 are SOP lines: policy and who decides. 2 and 4 are work-instruction lines: exact tools and known errors. ::: ## An SOP, up close Here is the sales-order procedure as the AI reads it. At the top: what it is for, when it applies, and who decides what. ![](assets/images/bcsupplychain4/r4-sop-page-top.webp) *The written procedure for a draft sales order. "Decision rights" is the key line: the AI prepares the draft, a person posts it and approves special prices and credit exceptions* ![](assets/images/bcsupplychain4/r4-sop-page-steps.webp) *The steps, the guardrails and the human-only steps. Each step links to a work instruction with the exact calls* Here is the heart of that procedure in plain text, shortened: the table of facts the AI must have before it creates anything, and what to do when one is missing. | Fact | Source | If missing | |---|---|---| | Customer | look up the customer (number, blocked, credit limit) | ask if no match | | Item | look up the item (stock, list price) | ask if ambiguous | | Quantity | the request | **ask** | | Unit price | the request or the user | **ask**. The item list price is only a suggestion. A "special" or "agreed" price is not stored where the AI can read it, so ask | | Ship / order date | the request, otherwise today | state the date you used | | Stock | stock on hand on the item | warn if the quantity is more than stock, and ask about backorder | | Customer credit | credit limit and balance on the customer | a limit of 0 with a balance due is worth a flag. Never change the limit | One line under the table does most of the work: **"Ask all missing facts in ONE round. Do not ask for anything you can look up."** ## A work instruction, in full An SOP says what to do and who decides. A **work instruction** says exactly how: which tool, which fields, and what goes wrong. This is the one for creating a sales order with one line. The AI reads it before its first write. ![](assets/images/bcsupplychain4/r4-wi-sales-line-top.webp) *The top of the work instruction. The first line tells the AI which of two tools to use and why: the other one was rejected in a test run. Then the header call, the line call, and the read-back* ![](assets/images/bcsupplychain4/r4-wi-sales-line-errors.webp) *The error table. Each row is a mistake the AI made once, with the fix. The last two sections matter for prices: Business Central stores exactly the price it is sent, so a special price must always be sent, and read back* Most of the content of these pages came from the AI itself. It hit an error, found the fix, and the procedure told it to write the fix into the matching work instruction. I reviewed what it added and kept what was right. ### Fireside chat: the SOP and the work instruction *Tonight's talk: two documents, one task.* **The SOP:** I decide the policy. Ask the price, because a list price is only a suggestion. Never raise a credit limit. A person posts. **The work instruction:** And I decide the buttons. Use the child tool, not the flat one. `documentNumber` is not a property, so use `documentId`. Always send the price you were given. **The SOP:** You never say why. **The work instruction:** You never say how. When the AI hits an error, it writes the fix into *me*, not into you. **The SOP:** Fair. Reviewing what it added is my job, though. **The work instruction:** Then we agree. You say what and why, I say how, and a person checks the edits. ## The hand-over procedure One procedure applies to every task. It says how the AI must end: always in the same five parts, in plain words, so that a person can finish the job. ![](assets/images/bcsupplychain4/r4-handover-top.webp) * …(truncated)
